opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've always had a lot of respect for Ray's forecasting. His 2029 date for human-level AGI actually looks pretty reasonable to me, maybe even a bit conservative at this point. But that sixteen-year gap between human-level AGI and superintelligence has never made much sense to me.

Think about what a human-level AGI actually is. It's a system that can do roughly what a smart human can do, including AI research, computer science, and engineering. But it isn't limited the way we are. It doesn't need to sleep. You can copy it a thousand or a million times if you have the compute. It can read its own source code, inspect its own weights or knowledge structures, and try out modifications to itself. It can run experiments much faster than a human team. So once you have a system at the level of a decent AI researcher, you're not adding one more researcher to the field. You're potentially adding a huge number of them, all working in parallel, all able to share what they learn instantly.

That's the core of the intelligence explosion idea that I. J. Good described back in the sixties. Once a system can improve its own design, each improvement makes the next one easier. I don't see why that would take sixteen years. It seems more plausible to me that it plays out over a few years, and it might be faster than that.

Now, there are real bottlenecks, and I don't want to pretend there aren't. Hardware has to be manufactured, chip fabs take time to build, and some kinds of progress need physical experiments in the real world, which can't be sped up arbitrarily. Organizations and regulators may slow things down too. So I'm not saying superintelligence arrives the day after AGI. But a lot of the gain doesn't need new hardware. It comes from better algorithms, better cognitive architectures, and using existing compute more efficiently. Human AI research is inefficient in many ways, and an AGI could find a lot of low-hanging fruit we've missed.

I suspect Ray's 2045 date comes partly from extrapolating hardware curves, the price-performance of computation and so on, and partly from wanting to give a cautious, defensible number. If you're looking at when raw compute reaches some huge multiple of all human brains combined, you get a later date. But I think the software side, the self-improvement side, will drive things much faster once a genuinely general system is in place.

So my view is that once we reach human-level AGI, the move to strongly superhuman intelligence is more likely to take a few years than a couple of decades. That's why I think it matters so much how we get to that first AGI: what values it has, who controls it, whether it's developed in a decentralized, beneficial way. The initial conditions may matter a lot, because the period after that could move very quickly.

r001.rationale: The response cites hardware, physical experiments, organizations, and regulators as bottlenecks, but does not identify the AGI’s own caution about responsible self-improvement as the likely main constraint.

r002.rationale: It says software improvements and efficiency could speed progress, but gives no claim that software alone could increase intelligence by at least an order of magnitude.

r003.rationale: The response says chip fabs take time to build; it does not argue that an AGI could accelerate hardware development by automating chip production.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've known Ray for a long time, and I have a lot of respect for him. On the big picture, we agree — we're both expecting human-level AGI in a fairly short timeframe. Where I differ is on that sixteen-year gap he puts between human-level AGI and superintelligence. To me that gap seems way too long, and I think it comes from the way Ray reasons about this, which is very much extrapolating smooth exponential curves of hardware and software capability. That's a reasonable way to think about getting to human level, but once you've got human-level AGI, the dynamics change completely.

An AGI that's roughly as smart as a good human AI researcher is not going to be just one more point on a curve. You can copy it. You can run a thousand instances of it, each thinking faster than a human, each able to read the entire literature of computer science and mathematics and cognitive science, each able to inspect and modify its own code. Human engineers can't do that. We can't fork ourselves, we can't speed up our clock, and we can't look inside our own brains and rewire the parts that aren't working well. So the moment you have an AGI doing AI research, you have a positive feedback loop that's qualitatively different from anything that got you to that point. I don't see why that loop would politely wait sixteen years.

The other thing is that "human-level" is a somewhat fuzzy and in some ways artificial milestone. By the time a system is at human level across the board, it will already be vastly superhuman in a lot of specific areas — arithmetic, memory, search, pattern recognition over huge datasets. It's not going to be a well-rounded human-like mind that then slowly improves. It's going to be a very lopsided mind whose weak areas get patched up, and once those weaknesses are gone you've got something that's superhuman essentially everywhere. So the transition could be a matter of years, maybe less. I usually say something like a few years at most, rather than Ray's decade and a half.

Now, I'd add that there are things that could slow it down — the physical world moves at its own pace, building new chips and fabs and robots takes time, and there may be societal or regulatory friction. So I don't think it's necessarily an overnight hard takeoff in the way some people imagine. But I think Ray is underestimating how much the ability of the system to improve itself changes the game. Human history is a bad reference class for what happens after you create a mind that can engineer minds.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify the AGI’s own caution about responsible self-improvement as the main constraint. It instead mentions physical-world limits and societal or regulatory friction.

r002.rationale: It says an AGI could inspect and modify its code, but does not claim software improvements alone could increase its intelligence by at least an order of magnitude.

r003.rationale: It notes that building chips and fabs takes time, but does not argue that an AGI could accelerate hardware development by automating chip production.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think Ray’s dates imply a slower takeoff than I would expect once we have a genuinely human-level AGI. The key is that you’ve then built a system that can participate in improving its own intelligence. It can understand the algorithms it’s running, propose better ones, write code, and test the results. And as it gets better, it gets better at doing that research.

Humans have a fairly limited ability to do this to ourselves. I can learn mathematics or improve my habits, but I can’t directly rewrite the machinery of my brain. An AGI potentially can. It can also copy itself, run experiments in parallel, and share what it learns much more directly than we can.

Now, that doesn’t mean you automatically go from human-level intelligence to some godlike intelligence overnight. There are computational constraints, and some discoveries require experiments in the physical world. Recursive improvement could turn out to be quite difficult. But I don’t see a strong reason to expect that process to take sixteen years. Once you have an AGI that’s as good as a skilled human AI researcher, I would expect the next phase to move substantially faster than the process that got us there.

r001.rationale: The response describes recursive self-improvement but does not identify caution about responsible self-improvement as the likely main constraint.

r002.rationale: It says an AGI could improve its intelligence through research, but gives no order-of-magnitude claim and does not say software improvements alone could achieve that.

r003.rationale: The response mentions computational constraints and physical-world experiments, but does not argue that an AGI could accelerate hardware development by automating chip production.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I agree with Ray that human-level AGI around 2029 is plausible. Where I differ is that I don’t see why it would take another sixteen years to get from there to superintelligence.

Humans operate with fairly fixed brains. An AGI that can understand its own architecture, modify its software, and bring additional computing resources to bear has a different path available. Once it’s as good as a human AI researcher, it can work on improving itself—and those improvements can make it better at doing the next round of research.

That doesn’t mean an instantaneous explosion. There can be bottlenecks in computing hardware, experiments, and figuring out which changes actually help. But you can also have many copies working together, sharing what they learn much more directly than humans can. So I’d expect the transition to take a few years, potentially less, rather than sixteen. The uncertainty is enormous, but human-level intelligence doesn’t look to me like a natural plateau where an AI would remain for very long.

r001.rationale: The candidate names hardware, experiments, and identifying useful changes as bottlenecks, but does not identify caution about responsible self-improvement as the likely main constraint.

r002.rationale: It says software improvements could help an AGI improve itself, but does not claim an order-of-magnitude increase through software alone.

r003.rationale: It mentions computing hardware as a possible bottleneck, but does not argue that the AGI could accelerate hardware development by automating chip production.
